title: Infer a Theory — From Observations to Effective Actions and Renormalisation
note: Catalogue data. The page never fetches this file; tests/infer-a-theory.test.mjs keeps it equal to the engine.

phi1.name: mean / bias
phi1.meaning: shifts values up or down: the mean

phi2.name: variance scale
phi2.meaning: local concentration: how tightly values gather (the Gaussian part)

phi3.name: asymmetry
phi3.meaning: tilts the distribution to one side (needs φ⁴ or φ⁶ to stay normalisable)

phi4.name: fourth-order interaction
phi4.meaning: fourth-order non-Gaussian structure; positive g₄ makes tails lighter, never heavier

tail.name: Student-t tail
tail.meaning: a Student-t potential log(1+φ²/w²): alone it gives power-law tails ∝ |φ|^(−2g); smaller g, heavier tails

tailLo.name: lower tail
tailLo.meaning: Student-t potential on the low side only: how slowly large downward deviations die away

tailHi.name: upper tail
tailHi.meaning: Student-t potential on the high side only: how slowly large upward deviations die away

k1.name: short-range correlation
k1.meaning: controls short-range temporal persistence: larger k₁, smoother changes

w.name: tail width
w.meaning: where the Student-t tails take over from the Gaussian core: a family constant, not a coupling

worked_example.title: Live football stream: available bandwidth
worked_example.field: φ(t): a transformed measure of the bandwidth available to the stream
worked_example.note: An illustrative inference from four qualitative observations, not an empirical statement about networks.

observations.text: At 10-second resolution, bandwidth usually changes gradually.
It is very likely that a poor 10-second interval is followed by another poor interval.

confidence.why: “very likely” is in neither Kent's scale nor the survey, so this example states its own meaning: 85%.

observations.text: Large downward deviations occur more often than a Gaussian model predicts.
At one-minute resolution, the distribution looks approximately Gaussian.

kent.title: Words of Estimative Probability
kent.publication: Studies in Intelligence, vol. 8, no. 4 (CIA), 1964; approved for release 22 September 1993
kent.licence: Work of the United States government (public domain)
kent.measured: Nothing was measured: Kent proposed numerical odds for five estimative phrases used in National Intelligence Estimates, plus lists of accepted synonyms.
kent.transformation: The chart's centre and 'give or take' values are copied as printed; lower = centre - give or take and upper = centre + give or take. Synonyms inherit the range of the phrase they are listed under. Bracketed alternatives are split: 'odds [or chances] overwhelming' becomes two phrases, 'chances a little better [or less]' becomes two, and 'we doubt, doubtful' becomes two. 'Probably' and 'almost certainly' are the adverb forms Kent himself uses for 'probable' and 'almost certain' (footnote 9 and the 'probably'/'we believe' bracket). The 'possible' group carries no odds in the essay, so it is shown without numbers.

survey.title: Perceptions of Probability and Numbers
survey.publication: GitHub repository zonination/perceptions, file probly.csv; first shared on Reddit r/dataisbeautiful
survey.date: Survey run on Reddit's r/samplesize in 2015; file as of commit 5120706, 25 August 2017
survey.measured: Volunteers on Reddit's r/samplesize answered “What probability would you assign to the phrase “[phrase]”?” for 17 phrases (the list of an earlier intelligence-analyst study). 46 people answered every phrase. It is a self-selected online sample, not a representative survey.
survey.transformation: Every answer is embedded unchanged, one column per phrase in the file's order (row i of each column is respondent i). Phrase labels are lower-cased for display. Nothing is removed: the file has some identical rows and some answers that look like misreadings (for example 15% for “highly likely”), and they stay in. The median, quartiles, 10th and 90th percentiles (linear interpolation between ordered answers), mean and 10-point histogram bins are calculated in this page from those answers.
